text.headline: The Cultural influences of wes anderson
text.text:
Wes Anderson is an American filmmaker who draws from different cultures in order to create distinctive styles for his movies. He takes influences from the architecture, cultures, and histories of different countries in order to create his own stylized worlds. 

This project shows the real-world influences and locations that inspired Wes Anderson's movies. This interactive map aims to show how cultural influences contribute to the unique feelings of the environments Anderson creates.

media.caption: Brookhaven Country Club scene (Contains explicit language)

text.headline: Bottle Rocket - Dallas, Texas
text.text:
The film Bottle Rocket draws inspiration from many areas in the Dallas and Fort-Worth areas, which isn't far from the city of Houston, Texas where Anderson was born. 

Located in Farmers Branch, Texas, Brookhaven Country Club appears in one of the highlight scenes from Wes Anderson's first feature film, Bottle Rocket. The film uses the golf course in the background to highlight the heightened status of James Caan and Bob Mapplethorpe.

media.caption: Jason Schwartzman in front of St. John's School

text.headline: Rushmore - Houston, Texas
text.text:
Wes Anderson's second feature film, Rushmore, was filmed primarily at St. John's School in Houston, Texas, which is Anderson's hometown.

Wes Anderson personally attended this school, and its traditional campus architecture helps to give the film a distinct, cozy feeling.

text.headline: The Royal Tenenbaums - New York city
text.text: Located in Harlem in the Borough of Manhattan, The Royal Tenenbaums was filmed in a Victorian-era mansion designed by architect Adolph Hoak. This house was chosen because Wes Anderson wanted the fictional family to have a sense of history while still showing how different all of the characters are. The history is shown through the architecture of the building, and the characters are separated into rooms that fit their distinctive quirks.

text.headline: The Life aquatic with steve zissou - New York city
text.text: Although the film features influences from coastal islands in Italy, the main journey of The Life Aquatic With Steve Zissou starts with The Explorer's Club. This building in New York City served as the inspiration for the fictional Explorers Club featured in the film . In real life, the organization is focused on scientific research, meaning the Explorers Club in the film does similar things.

text.headline: The darjeeling limited - Rajasthan, india
text.text: Starting with 2007's The Darjeeling Limited, Wes Anderson spread his sights wider and started to take influences from India. For this film in particular, Rajasthan India was a very important influence. While creating the movie, Anderson, Jason Schwartzman, and Roman Coppola travelled through India and their experiences helped shape the movie into what it became.

media.caption: Bill Murray on the set of Fantastic Mr. Fox

text.headline: Fantastic mr. Fox - GREAT MISSENDEN, ENGLAND
text.text:
Great Missenden was the main influence when creating Fantastic Mr. Fox, and the village holds a lot of significance. This area was home to Roald Dahl, the original writer of Fantastic Mr. Fox. When writing the movie, Wes Anderson stayed in Dahl's former house, and incorporated elements from Dahl's office into the film. The English countryside is also seen often in the film, showing how much of an influence this area was on the movie.

This same location was also vital to the creation of 2023's short film, The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar, as it was focused on more of Dahl's short stories that drew influences from his household and office.

text.headline: Moonrise kingdom - Naushon Island, Massachusetts
text.text: Naushon Island, off the coast of Massachusetts, served as the main inspiration for the island of New Penzance in 2012's Moonrise Kingdom. Wes Anderson originally travelled to this island and was interested in its isolated feeling, limited development, and unique atmosphere. His main goal was to portray the feeling of summer life as a child in 1960s New England.

media.caption: Cinematography from The Grand Budapest Hotel

text.headline: The Grand Budapest Hotel - Görlitz, Germany
text.text: For 2014's The Grand Budapest Hotel, Wes Anderson and his production designers took great inspiration from the architecture of Görlitz, Germany. During the production of the film, designers explored Central Europe and drew inspiration from the cozy culture and colorful architecture.

media.caption: The Brick Mansion from Isle of Dogs

text.headline: isle of Dogs - Tokyo, japan
text.text: For Anderson's second feature-length stop-motion film, he drew inspirations from Tokyo, Japan and decided to set it in a futuristic, dystopian setting. One of the major locations that influenced this film was The Imperial Hotel, which inspired the Brick Mansion, one of the main locations from the movie.  This film also drew from more than just architectural influences, as references to Japanese cinema, and culture are displayed throughout the film.

text.headline: The French Dispatch - Angoulême, France
text.text: Angoulême, France served as the inspiration for 2021's The French Dispatch, as well as the filming location for the fictional city of Ennui-sur-Blasé in the film. Anderson and his set designers were drawn to the city for its exaggerated architecture, featuring winding streets, steep staircases, and historic architecture. The production of this film included real-life buildings as for its sets, making the movie feel authentic.

text.headline: Asteroid city - Chinchón, Spain
text.text: While this film takes place in a desert town in the American Southwest, the filming took place in Cinchón, Spain. This area's seemingly endless desert, clear skies, and colored soil were accomplished through forced perspective and set design, helping to sell the illusion of being set in America, when finding a filming location similar to this in the states would be nearly impossible. Wes Anderson designed the town's buildings specifically for this film, giving it a unique atmosphere.

text.headline: The Phoenician Scheme - Villa Farnesina, Italy
text.text: Villa Farnesina is a Renaissance villa in Rome, Italy that served as the main inspiration for the mansion of Zsa-zsa in The Phoenician Scheme. Anderson and production designers studied different Italian villas for inspiration while designing the mansion, including staples of the architecture such as elaborate interiors and grand appearances. The film exaggerates details drawn from real cultural influences, giving it a unique and whimsical feeling.
